Thanks for making the time, Gisele. Let us start simple — walk me through your background.
I spent eighteen years at a bank in Brazil. I was responsible for the internal systems, and for the last six years I took ownership of the migration project.
That is a real track record. Tell me about a time when you made something simpler for the people who actually used it.
We streamlined the approval process. It went from six days to two, and the stakeholders were branch managers, not engineers, so I had to explain it in their words.
Good. Now, I see a gap after the bank. What have the last few months been?
A career break. My husband was transferred to Washington, I worked out my notice period, and we moved with our daughters. The break was a decision, not an accident.
Fair enough. One hypothetical, then the last five minutes are yours: what would you do if the team disagreed with you about a deadline?
I would ask what they can see that I cannot. If the date still had to move, I would say it early — I wouldn’t wait until the last week. And my question: what does onboarding look like here?
I was responsible for the internal systems of a bank for eighteen years.
I took a career break when we moved to Washington.
I wouldn't wait until the last week to say the date has to move.
What would onboarding look like in the first month?

Hi, before we go any further, let me tell you how this actually works here, because people always ask. There are three steps. First, a twenty-minute call with me, and that one is really just to check that the role and your track record line up. Then the hiring manager, his name is Paul, and that conversation is a full hour, and it is the one that matters. Last, a short chat with two people you would work with every day, and honestly, that one is about whether you would be a good fit. The whole thing takes about three weeks. What do I look at first? Not the school. I look at what you took ownership of, and whether you can explain it in plain words. And the biggest mistake, by far? Candidates who never ask anything. At the end I always say, do you have any questions for me, and half of them say no. Please do not be that person.

Hi Gisele, this is Mark Dyson from Halston Group. I am calling about the systems analyst role in Washington, the hybrid one you applied to on Tuesday. So, good news, the hiring manager wants to talk. I am going to try you again tomorrow morning, around ten your time, and if you miss me, do not worry, I will leave the number again. Two things I need from you by email before that call. One, a one-page version of your resume. One page, I mean it, nobody reads three. And two, just a line or two about your notice period, or, in your case, about when you would actually be able to start, since I understand you have been on a career break. Send those over by Thursday at five, because the team closes the list on Friday and I would hate for you to miss it. Okay, talk tomorrow. Bye.

Can I tell you the thing I wish somebody had told me? Stop apologizing for the gap. I hear it in every second interview, I am sorry, I was out for a year, and the apology does more damage than the year ever did. A career break is a line on a page. What people actually want to know is whether you are still the person who takes ownership of things, and eighteen months at home does not change that. And here is what nobody says out loud. Starting over in a country that is not yours is the hardest project management job there is. New systems, new language, a whole family to move, everything late and nothing where you left it. That is not a hole in your track record. Those are transferable skills, and they are the ones that never show up on anybody's resume. So say it like a fact. I took a career break. Here is what I did with it.
